question: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 6-day history of gradually worsening left knee pain. The pain is exacerbated by movement and kneeling. There is no pain at rest and no history of trauma to the knee. He is concerned because his soccer tryouts are in a few days. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows mild swelling and tenderness to palpation of the left anterior, superior tibia. Extension of the left knee against resistance reproduces the knee pain; flexion is limited by pain. There is no local erythema or effusion of the left knee. A lateral view of an x-ray of his left knee is shown. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?

options.opa: Impingement of the infrapatellar fat pad
options.opd: Traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle

enhanced_information: The most likely underlying cause of the patient's symptoms is traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle, supported by the clinical presentation of gradually worsening left knee pain exacerbated by movement, tenderness to palpation of the tibia, and reproduction of pain with knee extension. The evidence paths do not provide additional relevant information in this context.
analysis: The patient's presentation of gradually worsening left knee pain exacerbated by movement, tenderness to palpation of the tibia, and reproduction of pain with knee extension is highly suggestive of traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle, also known as Osgood-Schlatter disease. This condition commonly affects active adolescents during their growth spurt, causing pain at the tibial tubercle due to repetitive stress on the patellar tendon insertion. The absence of local erythema or effusion makes other options less likely.
